title: Leader of Canadian Tories Supports " Decriminalization " Not " Legalization " -- Again. This Makes Mere " Decriminalization " a Defeat for Us. Defining Our Terms and Setting Our Goals.

content_html_sanitized:
Posted May 23, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: As you will see below, the leader of the Canadian Progressive Conservative [Tory] Party, former Prime Minister Joe Clark, has again come out in favor of the " decriminalization " of marijuana, but not its " legalization ".

With the leader of this party supporting decriminalization, clearly that is not a worthy goal for us. Only full legalization should be acceptable.

As I wrote on Monday, I think that ending marijuana prohibition in Canada in two years is a realistic goal, but we need to understand the various alternatives, define our terms and set our goals.

Last week, the Journal of the Canadian Medical Association endorsed " decriminalization " – meaning possession would not be fully legal, but would be treated like a traffic offense, subject only to a small fine.

This evening I received an email from a Pot-TV viewer who asked some very timely questions about the difference between " decriminalization " and " legalization. "

" I have heard many people use the teams interchangeably and its important to use the correct term….any info about this issue would be appreciated "

He was kind enough to send along some dictionary definitions.

Amusingly, Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary’s definition of decriminalize included this example: " to remove or reduce the criminal classification or status of; especially : to repeal a strict ban on while keeping under some form of regulation <decriminalize the possession of marijuana. "

How thoughtful of Merriam-Webster!

In fact, these are terms that do not have precise definitions – especially in the context of marijuana prohibition. As our viewer noted, they are sometimes used interchangeably, but they should not be.

There is really no point in categorizing all of the errors; however, people should pay careful attention to determine what the speaker – writer – really means. As the song says, words sometimes have two meanings.

" Decriminalization " usually means the absence of criminal -- but not civil -- penalties for possession of a small amount of marijuana for " personal use. " That is usually an ounce, but not always.

" Decriminalization " also necessarily means leaving production and sales in the black market, which is a disastrous social policy. That is a point that we have to make at every opportunity.

" Legalization " usually means some form of " regulated " sales. In fact, " legalization " generally implies something like the alcohol and tobacco models.

There are those who would favor no laws at all for marijuana. This is sometimes called the " tomato model. " Anyone can sell tomatoes to anyone, at any time. That is very unlikely for marijuana for the foreseeable future. It is almost certain that there will be age restrictions, etc.

In The Netherlands marijuana is still kept technically – de jure -- illegal to comply with international treaties, but personal possession and small scale sales are de facto legal, and subject to regulation. Very Dutch.

Consequently, some reformers argue that we should use the word " regulate " to make clear the distinction between the chaos of prohibition and the control of regulated markets. They have a point. Others simply try to avoid the term.

For too long, these definitions have been largely of academic significance. We were lucky to get " decriminalization " -- however it was defined. But in Canada and in some countries in Europe, that is no longer the case.

Now we need to come up with precise policy recommendations. Over the next several months we will be preparing a range of possible models for legalization. This is necessary simply to show the Canadian politicians that these are questions to which many people have already given much thought, even if they have not.

Well, so much for definitions, now for goals.

In Canada, full legalization is the only acceptable goal. At this point, decriminalization would be a defeat. After all, when the head of the Tories wants " decriminalization " that should be a given.

Personally, I have always made very clear that I am in favor of the " legalization " of marijuana, -- using, growing, and selling. I think that some regulation is inevitable, so I see no point in even trying for the " tomato model. " The really important battle will be around age restrictions and avoiding over-regulation, especially government monopolies. I think that the " coffee-shop " model is ideal.

Unfortunately, the appalling people who govern DEAland will want to keep the age for cannabis the same as it is for alcohol, 21, so it will be difficult to keep young people out of the black market. Of course, by the time marijuana prohibition ends in DEAland the prohibitionists will be so discredited that this particular stupidity may also end.

In any case, the job before us is clear. We must bring about the legalization of marijuana in Canada, using, growing, selling. That is the minimum definition of success.)


Clark supports decriminalizing marijuana

As he has done several times during his political career, Tory Leader Joe Clark called Tuesday for the decriminalization of marijuana.

" I believe the least controversial approach is decriminalization because it's unjust to see someone, because of one decision one night in their youth, carry the stigma — to be barred from studying medicine, law, architecture or other fields where a criminal record could present an obstacle, " Mr. Clark said while on a visit to Quebec.

" I'm making a distinction between legalization and decriminalization. What interests me is decriminalization. "

Advocates of medical marijuana, well aware of Mr. Clark's past statements on decriminalization, were surprised and encouraged by his remarks. It's not the first time in the veteran politician's career that he took that argument.

In 1979

" Once we have dealt with economic and institutional changes, we intend to act on decriminalization in the first term of office of a new Government, " he wrote. " Any moves toward establishing a government system of distribution would have to be studied carefully in advance...We believe that government sales should be among the options examined. "

Last week, a unanimous motion was passed by all parties in the House of Commons to strike a committee to study the issue of non-medicinal drugs in Canada.

Increasingly, high profile politicians are voicing their support for decriminalization of marijuana. Last week, federal Justice Minister Anne McLellan said she was " quite open " to a debate on the issue. Health Minister Allan Rock has also said he supports medicinal use and Canadian Alliance Leader Stockwell Day has admitted he smoked pot in his youth.

And last week, an editorial in the Canadian Medical Association Journal advocated the decriminalization of marijuana possession for personal use.

" My opinion is not necessarily shared by all the members of my party, but it's the sort of approach we will favour before the committee, " Mr. Clark said.

Marijuana advocates were surprised and mostly positive about Mr. Clark's support for decriminalization.

Dana Larsen, editor of Cannabis Culture magazine and Deputy Leader of the B.C. Marijuana Party, said " I'm glad to hear him say this. I do think the Tories believe [cannabis] should be decriminalized. "

" Anything they do not to put people in jail is a step in the right direction. "

The party, running in its first election, got 3.2 per cent of the vote in last week's B.C. election, but Mr. Larsen said the support points to increasing effort by political parties to put decriminalization on their agendas.

Mr. Larsen said politicians are forced to play catch-up, as court decisions and compassion clubs show that public support is increasing.

He said Ottawa has studied the issue and now it's time to act. Although he doesn't think marijuana will be decriminalized without " a great deal of effort, " he said that it's accepted that " medicinal marijuana " can aid those in chronic pain.

Philip McMillan, the facilities director for the Nelson Cannabis Compassion Club in British Columbia, said marijuana is becoming acceptable by all classes of people, pointing to the discussions in right-wing parties.

A poll released Tuesday reported that Canadians are now evenly split on legalizing the drug, compared with 26-per-cent support 1975.

The United States, meanwhile, is coming down hard on illegal drugs. Last Tuesday, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that pot pharmacies are no longer allowed to legally grow and distribute medicinal marijuana.

The Ultimate Hypocrisy: " Justice " Thomas, Who Smoked Marijuana At Yale Law School, Writes Supreme Court Opinion Against Medical Cannabis. Drug War Depends Upon Persecution of Sick and Dying.

But other countries are taking the opposite approach. In January, the Belgian government agreed to decriminalize the use of marijuana, following a similar decision in the Netherlands.

Philippe Lucas, director of the Vancouver Island Compassion Society, has heard enough talk. " I think it's good that this discussion and debate is to go on, but we've been here before, " he said. " It's now time for action. "
